rationale: A wins because it keeps the story closer to what can actually be reported. "Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally" turns the launch into a concrete distribution question and names the proof that would make or break it. B has real instincts, but "The bank Silicon Valley Bank's collapse built is becoming a mass-market consumer bank" is the kind of overreach that gets a founder embarrassed on follow-up: Mercury is not a chartered bank, and invite-only is not mass-market.
gaps_in_A: "Mercury's name recognition was built entirely on being the startup-banking alternative" overstates the supplied fact. The update says Mercury became well known after SVB, not that SVB built the whole brand.

"The hook is directional: Mercury's playbook runs opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried" imports industry context the update did not provide. A correctly asks for comparables, but the line still gets ahead of the evidence.
"can leverage that trust" is banned-word mush. Say "use" or, better, prove whether trust transfers at all.

"Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally" is a little too certain. The facts give the customer base and a waitlist, not confirmation that existing business customers are being targeted first.
gaps_in_B: "The bank Silicon Valley Bank's collapse built" is wrong twice. Mercury is not a bank charter, and the facts say SVB made Mercury well known, not that it built the company.
"mass-market consumer bank" is invented. The product is initially invite-only with a waitlist; that is not mass-market.

"a subject depositors got a real education in when SVB collapsed" blurs SVB's chartered-bank failure with fintech partner-bank custody risk. Same broad world, different mechanism. Reporters will notice.
"When a business-only fintech decides it's ready to be a full-service bank" overclaims the product. Checking and savings through partner banks does not equal a full-service bank.
